questions.question: What two rules must a linear map $A:V\to W$ satisfy?
The image (range) of a linear map $A\colon V\to W$ is a subspace of:
What does homogeneity say about $A(\lambda u)$?
options: The scalar is added after applying $A$.
The scalar must be sent to zero.
The scalar can be pulled outside: $A(\lambda u)=\lambda Au$.

questions.question: Why is knowing a linear map on a basis enough?
options: Linear maps are defined only on finite sets.
Basis vectors must all be mapped to zero.
Every vector in the domain is a linear combination of basis vectors.
A linear map ignores all vectors outside the basis, under all circumstances whatsoever.

questions.question: What kind of object is $\mathcal L(V,W)$?
options: The kernel of a fixed map from $V$ to $W$.
The vector space of all linear maps from $V$ to $W$.
The list of basis vectors of $W$.

questions.question: Which map $A:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ is linear?
Which rule fails for $T(x)=x+1$ as a map $\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$?
options: It maps every vector to zero, for every possible choice of input.

questions.question: For a linear map $A$ with $A(e_1)=(1,0)$ and $A(e_2)=(0,3)$, what is $A(2e_1-e_2)$?
Why is the zero map $0(v)=0$ linear?
options: It satisfies both additivity and homogeneity.
It sends no vector to a vector.
It is linear only when $v$ is nonzero.

questions.question: On polynomials, what is $D(3x^2+2x)$ for the derivative map $D(p)=p^{\prime}$?
What is the quickest way to disprove that a map is linear?
options: Show that the map has a name.
Find one violation of additivity or homogeneity.
Check that it has at least one output.
Find a basis for the codomain only.

questions.question: Why must the domain and codomain be vector spaces over the same field for linearity?
options: The same scalars must make sense in both $V$ and $W$ for homogeneity.
Addition is used only in the domain, never in the codomain.
The definition requires both spaces to have the same dimension.
The map must send every vector to a scalar.

questions.question: Additivity and homogeneity together are equivalent to which single condition?
Let $A:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ be $A(x,y)=x-y$. What is $A((1,2)+(3,4))$?
The composition of two linear maps is:
options: linear only if the maps are equal

questions.question: Every linear map between finite-dimensional spaces can be represented by a:
If a map satisfies $A(u+v)=Au+Av$ but not $A(\lambda u)=\lambda Au$, is it linear?
options: Yes, additivity alone is the full definition.
No, because no additive map can exist.

questions.question: Why does $A(0)=0$ follow for a linear map?
options: It follows only for maps into $\mathbb R$.
It follows only if the map is the identity.
It is an extra axiom unrelated to linearity.

questions.question: Which map $T:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ is not linear because it does not send $\boldsymbol0$ to $\boldsymbol0$?
